Chapter 4: Network Access

Physical layer protocols and principles — bandwidth, throughput and standards — network media (copper, UTP/STP, coaxial, fiber, wireless), data link sublayers, topologies and frame structures.

★ Revision kit — Chapter 4: Network Access

Eight structured sections for revision: overview, definitions, concept explanations, comparisons, important facts, a knowledge check, common misunderstandings and a quick revision read. Everything here is additive — the complete original slides follow below, unchanged, and every fact links back to its source slide.

1Chapter overviewFrom the course PDFs

Chapter 4 covers the bottom two layers in practice. 4.1 introduces the physical layer: its standards (RJ connectors, TIA-568 cabling, IEEE 802.3/802.11/802.15) and the principles of bandwidth and throughput. 4.2 is a survey of media — copper (UTP, STP, coaxial), fiber optic, and wireless — including UTP design/testing, fiber's four industry uses, a direct fiber-vs-copper comparison and the 802.11/802.15/802.16 wireless standards. 4.3 moves up to the data link layer: LLC and MAC sublayers, topologies, media-access methods (controlled vs contention), duplex, and the frame with its Layer 2 address.

Learning objectives

  • Explain the purpose of the physical layer and what its standards address (slides 4–6).
  • Distinguish bandwidth from throughput and name the factors that reduce throughput (slides 7–8).
  • Compare copper, fiber and wireless media: construction, properties, testing and standards (slides 11–26).
  • Describe the data link layer's sublayers (LLC and MAC) and how devices gain access to the media (slides 28–43).
  • Recognise frames and Layer 2 addressing, and relate the TCP/IP network access layer to OSI Layers 1–2 (slides 44–46).

Most important concepts

  • Physical layer standards — physical components, encoding technique, signaling method.
  • Throughput vs capacity — bits actually delivered per period, reduced by traffic and latency.
  • Copper vs fiber vs wireless — cost, distance, EMI immunity, skills.
  • LLC + MAC sublayers — LLC lets several protocols coexist on one network; MAC controls access.
  • Media access methods — controlled (no collisions, token) vs contention (CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA).
  • Frames & Layer 2 addresses — the data link PDU and its hardware identifiers.

2Key definitionsFrom the course PDFs

Physical layer (Layer 1)

Provides the means to transport the bits that make up a data link layer frame across the network media; its standards address physical components, frame encoding technique and signaling method. slide 46

Throughput

The number of bits transferred across the media over a given period of time; influenced by the amount of traffic, type of traffic, and latency/delays from the number of devices between source and destination. slide 8

EMI / RFIelectromagnetic / radio-frequency interference

Interference copper must be designed against; UTP counters it indirectly (cancellation, twist rates) rather than with a shield. slide 16

Crosstalk

Interference between wire pairs; limited by cancellation and by varying the number of twists per pair — a parameter checked when testing UTP. slide 16

UTPUnshielded Twisted Pair

The most common copper networking media; no shielding — instead cancellation and precise twist counts (pairs are twisted differently, e.g. orange less than blue) to limit crosstalk and outside EMI/RFI. slide 46

STPShielded Twisted Pair

Twisted pair with foil/braided shields around the pairs or cable to fight interference. slide 14

Coaxial cable

The third main copper type used in networking (with UTP and STP). slide 12

Attenuation

Loss of signal strength — one of the parameters a UTP tester measures (with wire map, cable length and crosstalk). slide 19

LLCLogical Link Control sublayer

Data link sublayer that makes it possible for several protocols to coexist and be transported over the same network. slide 29

MACMedia Access Control sublayer

Data link sublayer that controls how devices access the media; the method depends on topology and media sharing. slide 32

Topology (physical vs logical)

Physical topology = where devices/cables actually are; logical topology = how traffic is expected to flow (e.g. a logical point-to-point path may exist over media only one router uses). slide 35

Controlled access

Media access where only one station transmits at a time — others wait their turn, no collisions; may use token passing (Token Ring IEEE 802.5, FDDI). slide 40

Contention-based access

Media access where stations may transmit at any time, collisions exist, and mechanisms resolve contention: CSMA/CD for 802.3 Ethernet, CSMA/CA for 802.11 wireless. slide 41

Frame

The data link layer PDU; the physical layer transports its bits across the media. slide 46

Layer 2 address

The data link layer's address carried in frames (MAC addressing — see Chapter 5). slide 45

CSMA/CACarrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance

The access mechanism used by 802.11 wireless networks. slide 41

CSMA/CDCarrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection

The access mechanism used by 802.3 Ethernet networks. slide 41

3Concept explanationsStudy note

Why UTP works without a shield slide 16

UTP uses two tricks instead of shielding: cancellation — wires in a circuit are placed so their magnetic fields cancel each other (and outside EMI/RFI) — and controlled twist rates — precise twists per metre specified by standard (orange pair is twisted less than the blue pair).

Example: That's why untwisting a cable too far at the connector invites crosstalk — the design relies on the twists.

Reading the fiber-vs-copper table slide 24

Fiber wins on almost every physical property — distance (up to 100 km vs 1–100 m), EMI/electrical immunity (complete), bandwidth ceiling (100 Gbps vs 10 Gbps) — but loses on cost, installation skill and safety handling, which are 'highest' for fiber and 'lowest' for copper.

Example: Copper suits an office floor run; fiber suits a building backbone or links between cities.

Choosing an access method follows the topology slide 41

The MAC method depends on topology and media sharing. Shared-media designs that schedule turns (token ring/FDDI) give no collisions; Ethernet/Wi-Fi let anyone talk and resolve collisions: CD on wired, CA on wireless (CA because a wireless station cannot hear a collision while transmitting — avoidance instead).

Example: Same office, two technologies: an Ethernet hub segment uses CSMA/CD; the Wi-Fi association uses CSMA/CA.

Throughput is not the same as the label on the box slide 8

Throughput = bits actually transferred per period. It drops with (1) the amount of traffic, (2) the type of traffic, and (3) latency added by every device between source and destination — so a '1 Gbps' link can deliver far less in a busy, deeply nested path.

Example: A busy office link at peak hour: same hardware, lower throughput than at night.

LLC and MAC split the work slide 29

The data link layer splits into LLC (lets several protocols coexist and be transported over the same network) and MAC (decides how/when a device uses the media). Different MAC technologies sit under the same LLC: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi, 802.15 Bluetooth.

Example: One PC can use Ethernet and Wi-Fi simultaneously because LLC abstracts which MAC is underneath.

Physical layer standards you should recognise slide 6

ISO 8877 adopted RJ connectors (RJ-11, RJ-45); ISO 11801 is a network cabling standard similar to EIA/TIA 568; TIA-568-C is the telecommunications cabling standard used by nearly all voice/video/data networks (RJ-45 pinouts); TIA-598-C fiber color coding; TIA-942 data centre infrastructure; G.992 ADSL; IEEE 802.3/802.11/802.15 Ethernet/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth.

Example: A cabling exam question about pinouts points to TIA-568-C; fiber colour coding points to TIA-598-C.

Technical terms are kept exactly as the course uses them; the plain-language wording and examples are supplementary study notes.

5Important factsFrom the course PDFs

  • Physical layer standards address three areas: physical components, frame encoding technique, signaling method. slide 46
  • Standards: ISO 8877 (RJ connectors), ISO 11801 (cabling, like EIA/TIA 568), TIA-568-C (cabling, RJ-45 pinouts), TIA-569-B (pathways/spaces), TIA-598-C (fiber color coding), TIA-942 (data centres), G.992 (ADSL), IEEE 802.3/802.11/802.15. slide 6
  • Throughput factors: amount of traffic, type of traffic, latency/delays from the number of devices between source and destination. slide 8
  • Three copper types: UTP, STP, coaxial; UTP is the most common. slide 46
  • Every copper termination is a point of possible signal loss and noise introduction. slide 17
  • UTP test parameters: wire map, cable length, attenuation (signal loss), crosstalk. slide 19
  • Fiber's four industry uses: enterprise backbones, FTTH/access (always-on broadband), long-haul (ISP/inter-country), submarine. slide 20
  • Wireless concerns: coverage area, interference, security. slide 25
  • 802.11 variants: a = 54 Mbps/5 GHz; b = 11 Mbps/2.4 GHz; g = 54 Mbps/2.4 GHz (b-compatible); n = 600 Mbps (2.4 & 5 GHz); ac = 1 Gbps/5 GHz; ad = 7 Gbps (2.4/5/60 GHz). slide 26
  • IEEE 802.15 (Bluetooth): up to 3 Mb/s, pairing over 1–100 m; IEEE 802.16: up to 1 Gbps, point-to-multipoint wireless broadband. slide 26
  • Data link layer splits into LLC and MAC; LLC enables several protocols to coexist over the same network; related families: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi, 802.15 Bluetooth. slide 29
  • Token passing examples: Token Ring (IEEE 802.5), FDDI — controlled access with no collisions. slide 40
  • The TCP/IP network access layer equals OSI Layer 2 + Layer 1. slide 46

6Knowledge checkPractice

8 practice questions — a mix of multiple-choice, true/false, short-answer and explanation tasks. Answers stay hidden until you reveal them, and each one explains why it is correct. These are revision questions written for this site from the course content — they are not lecturer instructions or examination questions.

Multiple choiceQ1. Which standard gives the RJ-45 pinouts used by nearly all voice, video and data networks?

  • A. TIA-568-C
  • B. TIA-598-C
  • C. ISO 8877
  • D. G.992
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — TIA-568-C

Why: Slide 6: TIA-568-C is the telecommunications cabling standard used by nearly all voice/video/data networks (568-C: RJ-45 pinouts). TIA-598-C is fiber colour coding, ISO 8877 adopted RJ connectors, G.992 is ADSL.

True or falseQ2. UTP cable counters EMI/RFI with a foil shield wrapped around its pairs.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: False

Why: UTP does not use shielding — it relies on cancellation and precise twist rates (slide 16). The foil/braided shields describe STP (slide 14).

Short answerQ3. List the four parameters a UTP cable tester should check after installation.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Wire map (proper pin termination, shorts), cable length, signal loss due to attenuation, and crosstalk.

Why: Slide 19 lists exactly these four.

Multiple choiceQ4. Which access mechanism is used by 802.11 wireless networks?

  • A. CSMA/CD
  • B. CSMA/CA
  • C. Token passing
  • D. FDDI
Show answer & explanation

Answer: B — CSMA/CA

Why: Slide 41: CSMA/CD for 802.3 Ethernet, CSMA/CA for 802.11 wireless. Token passing (Token Ring, FDDI) is the controlled-access alternative.

True or falseQ5. In a controlled-access method such as token passing, collisions cannot occur because only one station transmits at a time.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: True

Why: Slide 40: one station at a time, devices wait their turn, no collisions.

Short answerQ6. Name the three main types of copper media used in networking.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Unshielded twisted pair (UTP), shielded twisted pair (STP), and coaxial cable.

Why: Summary slide 46 states all three and notes UTP is the most common.

ExplanationQ7. A network needs a 5 km link between two buildings with heavy electrical machinery nearby. Using the chapter's fiber-vs-copper table, justify fiber.

Show answer & explanation

Answer: Distance: copper is 'relatively short (1–100 m)' while fiber reaches 1–100,000 m, so 5 km rules copper out. EMI: copper's EMI/RFI immunity is low, fiber is completely immune — essential near electrical machinery. The trade-off is cost, installation skill and safety precautions, which are highest for fiber.

Why: All four points come straight from the Fiber versus Copper table (slide 24).

Multiple choiceQ8. What is the main purpose of the LLC sublayer?

  • A. To make several protocols coexist and be transported over the same network
  • B. To detect collisions on Ethernet
  • C. To encode bits onto the media
  • D. To assign IP addresses to hosts
Show answer & explanation

Answer: A — protocols coexisting on one network

Why: Slide 29: LLC 'makes it possible for several protocols to coexist and to be transported over the same network'.

7Common misunderstandingsStudy note

"Unshielded" = unprotected against interference

UTP has no shield but is engineered against EMI/RFI/crosstalk via cancellation and twist rates; STP instead adds foil/braided shields (slides 12–16).

Bandwidth = what you actually get (throughput)

Throughput is the measured bits transferred per period, reduced by traffic volume, traffic type and latency from intermediate devices (slide 8) — it is the real-world figure, not the link's headline capability.

All networks handle collisions the same way

No: controlled access (token) has no collisions; contention-based Ethernet uses CSMA/CD and wireless uses CSMA/CA — different mechanisms for shared media (slides 40–41).

Physical topology = logical topology

Physical = where devices/cables are; logical = how traffic is expected to flow. The chapter's point-to-point slides show a logical path can differ from who physically owns the media (slides 33–36).

8Quick revision (2–5 minutes)Study note

  • Layer 1: transports the bits of data link frames; standards cover physical components, encoding and signaling (RJ via ISO 8877; TIA-568-C pinouts; TIA-598-C fiber colours; 802.3/802.11/802.15).
  • Throughput = bits per period; drops with traffic amount, traffic type and device latency.
  • Copper: UTP (most common; cancellation + twists, no shield), STP (shielded), coax. Test UTP for wire map, length, attenuation, crosstalk — every termination risks loss/noise.
  • Fiber: longer reach (to 100 km), 100 Gbps, fully immune to EMI/electrical hazards — but highest cost/skill/safety needs; used in backbones, FTTH, long-haul, submarine.
  • Wireless: concerns = coverage, interference, security; 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ad (up to 7 Gbps), 802.15 Bluetooth (3 Mb/s, 1–100 m), 802.16 (1 Gbps point-to-multipoint). Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA.
  • Layer 2: LLC (protocols coexist) + MAC (media access: controlled/token — no collisions — vs contention CSMA/CD|CA); frames carry Layer 2 addresses; TCP/IP network access layer = OSI L1 + L2.

Slide 16
UTP Cabling

Properties of UTP Cabling

UTP cable does not use shielding to counter the effects of EMI

(electric magnetic interference) and RFI (radio frequency

interference). Instead, cable designers have discovered that they

can limit the negative effect of crosstalk by:

  • Cancellation: when two wires in an electrical circuit are placed

close together, their magnetic fields are the exact opposite of

each other. Therefore, the two magnetic fields cancel each other

out and also cancel out any outside EMI and RFI signals.

  • Varying the number of twists per wire pair: UTP cable must follow precise specifications governing how many twists or braids are permitted per meter (3.28 feet) of cable.
  • The orange/orange white pairs are twisted less than the blue/white blue pair.

Testing UTP Cables

Fiber Optic Cabling

Properties of Fiber Optic Cabling

Fiber-optic cabling is now being used in four types of industry:

  • Enterprise Networks (backbone)
  • Fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) and Access Networks (always-on broadband services)
  • Long-Haul Networks (ISP use it to connect to countries)
  • Submarine Networks (harsh under sea environments)

Slide 26
Wireless Media

Types of Wireless Media

  • IEEE 802.11 standards
  • Commonly referred to as Wi-Fi.
  • Uses CSMA/CA
  • Variations include:
  • 802.11a: 54 Mbps, 5 GHz - business
  • 802.11b: 11 Mbps, 2.4 GHz - home
  • 802.11g: 54 Mbps, 2.4 GHz – compatible with b
  • 802.11n: 600 Mbps, 2.4 and 5 GHz
  • 802.11ac: 1 Gbps, 5 GHz
  • 802.11ad: 7 Gbps, 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 60 GHz
  • IEEE 802.15 standard
  • Supports speeds up to 3 Mb/s
  • Provides device pairing over distances from 1 to 100 meters.
  • IEEE 802.16 standard
  • Provides speeds up to 1 Gbps
  • Uses a point-to-multipoint topology to provide wireless broadband access.

Chapter 4 Summary

1 slide
Slide 46
Network Access

Summary

  • The TCP/IP network access layer is the equivalent of the OSI data link layer (Layer 2) and the physical layer (Layer 1).
  • The OSI physical layer provides the means to transport the bits that make up a data link layer frame across the network media.
  • The physical layer standards address three functional areas: physical components, frame encoding technique, and signaling method.
  • Using the proper media is an important part of network communications. Without the proper physical connection, either wired or wireless, communications between any two devices will not occur.
  • Wired communication consists of copper media and fiber cable.
  • There are three main types of copper media used in networking: unshielded-twisted pair (UTP), shielded-twisted pair (STP), and coaxial cable. UTP cabling is the most common copper networking media.

Network Access
Summary
The TCP/IP network access layer is the equivalent of the OSI data link 
layer (Layer 2) and the physical layer (Layer 1).
The OSI physical layer provides the means to transport the bits that make 
up a data link layer frame across the network media. 
The physical layer standards address three functional areas: physical 
components, frame encoding technique, and signaling method.
Using the proper media is an important part of network communications. 
Without the proper physical connection, either wired or wireless, 
communications between any two devices will not occur.
Wired communication consists of copper media and fiber cable.
There are three main types of copper media used in networking: 
unshielded-twisted pair (UTP), shielded-twisted pair (STP), and coaxial 
cable. UTP cabling is the most common copper networking media.
